name: Isomorphic Labs
blurb: Alphabet's AI drug design company and its funding.
title: Isomorphic Labs
answer: Isomorphic Labs was spun out of Google DeepMind to turn AlphaFold class models into a drug design engine. It has partnerships with major drugmakers and has raised $600 million in 2025 and a further $2.1 billion in 2026 to scale the engine and take its own candidates into the clinic.

reading.body:
Isomorphic Labs has raised $2.7 billion across two rounds to turn AlphaFold-class models into drugs, and its first clinical data will be the real test of that bet.

The company was spun out of Google DeepMind in 2021 and sits inside Alphabet, separate from but closely linked to DeepMind. It does not sell model access. Its route to market is drug discovery partnerships plus its own pipeline, which means revenue depends on molecules working in humans rather than on licensing software.

The funding pattern is the notable part. A $600 million first external round in 2025, then $2.1 billion in 2026, is a large step up before any clinical readout is recorded here. That scale of capital is what it costs to run a design engine and push candidates toward the clinic, and it shows investors pricing structure-based design as a platform rather than a single programme.

What the data does not cover is whether any of it works. There is no trial result, no candidate count, no partner named, and no compute or power figure attached to the engine. The clinical endpoint is stated as the test and remains unpassed.

explainer:
Isomorphic Labs was founded in 2021 by Demis Hassabis as a sister company to Google DeepMind, with the aim of turning advances in protein structure prediction into a general engine for designing medicines. It co-developed AlphaFold 3 with DeepMind and has used its models to work on its own internal programmes and with pharmaceutical partners.

Its funding marks how much the market expects from structure based AI design. The company raised 600 million dollars in 2025, its first outside funding, and a further 2.1 billion dollars in 2026. Like other AI drug designers it ultimately has to prove itself in the clinic, where molecules designed with its engine will be judged by the same standards as any other drug candidate.

Where Isomorphic came from

Isomorphic Labs was founded in 2021 as a sister company to Google DeepMind, led by DeepMind's chief executive Demis Hassabis, to apply the AlphaFold line of protein structure models to drug discovery. AlphaFold solved a decades old problem, predicting a protein's three dimensional shape from its sequence, and the later versions extended that to how proteins interact with other molecules, including potential drugs. Isomorphic's premise is that models of that kind can replace much of the trial and error in finding a molecule that binds a target.

What it does differently

Most AI drug discovery companies build on public structure data and their own experiments. Isomorphic builds on the models that produced the structure data, with the research team that made them, and it has signed research partnerships with large pharmaceutical companies to work on targets they bring. It has also raised substantial outside investment to build its own pipeline. The company has described its ambition as reducing the time to find a candidate drug from years to months, a claim that will only be tested when its molecules reach and pass clinical trials.

Why it is watched closely

Isomorphic is the clearest test of whether a frontier AI lab can turn a scientific breakthrough into medicines. If its partnered programmes produce clinical candidates on the promised timelines, the economics of early discovery change for everyone. If they do not, it will suggest that structure prediction, while valuable, was not the bottleneck. Either way, the results over the next few years will shape how much the industry invests in this approach.
